prospect.name: Tyron Giuliani
prospect.occupation: Semi-retired; founded a business with his wife and sold it to a public company last year; also does some consulting
prospect.family_status: Married, two children (he states 8 and 10-11 at one point and 11 and 9 at another)
prospect.training_background: Ex-army (enlisted pre-1998, left at 24). Long yo-yo history between roughly 74 kg and 130 kg over 15 years. Currently two 1.5-hour sessions per week with a personal trainer doing functional work, lighter weights and balance; chiropractor roughly weekly; previously cycling three days a week plus upper-body weights twice a week before medication changes. No kettlebell experience.
prospect.medical: PTSD from army service with nightmares and recurrent depressive episodes; sees a psychiatrist roughly weekly. Bilateral compartment syndrome in all four compartments of both legs plus popliteal entrapment — three surgeries, all failed; walking beyond about 10,000 steps or on uneven ground causes significant pain. Rotator cuff injury of roughly 20 years. On heavy pain medication that he says caused a 5-10% weight gain and heavy sedation; sleeps until 10-11am, cannot sleep until 2-3am. Previously on Ozempic for a couple of months without effect; about to start Mounjaro.

signals: Three failed surgeries for bilateral compartment syndrome and popliteal entrapment; cannot run or do sustained cardio
Explicitly asks whether kettlebells are safe for him given a 20-year rotator cuff injury
No price resistance and states 'I have money, I have a good life'
Overlaps with the_rebuilder — he wants a former self back after a hard season — but the binding constraint is clinical, not motivational

goals.text: Get back down to 75-80 kg and, crucially, maintain it rather than yo-yo again
Find something sustainable that becomes part of the routine for the long run, not just six months
Be a fit dad his kids can model, and stop his less-active child inheriting his habits
Add a strength/muscle-building modality he can do at home alongside his functional PT work
Move and train without triggering leg and back pain

pains.text: Fifteen years of yo-yo weight between roughly 74 kg and 130 kg; reaches a goal, declares he will never go back, and is back within three years
PTSD and recurrent depressive episodes derail training for a week or two at a time and drive night eating
Bilateral compartment syndrome and popliteal entrapment with three failed surgeries; 10,000 steps means a day of pain, cardio and running are effectively unavailable
New pain medication controls the pain but caused significant weight gain and heavy sedation, cutting training volume to two sessions a week
Cannot sleep until 2-3am, wakes from nightmares, sleeps until 10-11am and naps during the day
Disciplined during the day, then snacks late at night — toast at 2am, and multiple pieces of the sweets his kids bring home
Accountability is entirely external — reports weight to his wife daily, relies on the PT — and results disappear when that accountability stops
Lives in downtown Tokyo surrounded by a 7-Eleven, an Italian restaurant and constant food temptation
Turning 52 in November and feels he has only a couple of cycles left before it is too late

objections.raw_quote: I haven't done the, what is it, cowbell, I haven't done the cowbells before. I wonder if them, or if they are okay. I've got a rota cuff injury, but that's been for 20 years.
objections.rep_response: Did not answer at the time. Much later asserted that kettlebells force the body to move as a unit, that Trevor can work around injuries and will modify any painful movement, and that many injured clients end up in less pain. Never asked whether any clinician had cleared loaded kettlebell work.

objections.raw_quote: The, you know, I draw lines in the sand and then I'll, you know, scuff them out when I get there. And like, I will extend that a little bit longer. So, you know, I've, you know, I've done, I've done the cycles. This is the thing I've done. I've done the cycles quite a few times.
objections.rep_response: Told him to give himself grace, then ran a Tony Robbins analogy about how long you give a baby to learn to walk and how you would never stop trying; concluded that he simply had not yet found the sustainable thing.

evidence: Call ended abruptly for a dentist appointment: 'I had this scheduled in for 45 minutes. I've got a, uh, I've stopped at 10, and I've got to go to the dentist.'
Prospect asked to continue: 'Yeah, I've got to hop off now, but can we speak more? Is that possible?'
Rep moved the calendar event and booked the same time the next day on the same Zoom link
Counter-evidence on any read of momentum: no price, no tiers and no close attempt occurred; only two of the three pillars were delivered
Counter-evidence on commitment: the prospect never gave a clean yes to the line-in-the-sand question and said he habitually scuffs the line out
outcome.next_step: Reconvene the following day at the same time on the same Zoom link to finish the presentation.

notable.note: Discovery call one of a multi-call sequence, all filed under the identical title 'Impromptu Zoom Meeting'. The rep ran an unusually strong consequence frame and root-cause section but skipped the commitment check entirely and moved into the pillar presentation on an explicitly hedged answer. The prospect is medically complex — PTSD, three failed lower-leg surgeries, popliteal entrapment, a 20-year rotator cuff injury and heavy sedating medication — and asked directly whether kettlebells were 'okay' for him. That question was never answered clinically and no clearance was sought. The rep also speculated that the programme might let him reduce his prescribed medication.

quality.notes: Several turns are merged across the speaker boundary. Clear instances: at 00:06:xx the prospect's monologue ends with the rep's line 'I'm sure that's pretty frustrating, I would imagine'; at 00:13:00 the rep's questions about semi-retirement are appended to the prospect's block; at 00:36:09 and 00:48:09 the rep's questions appear inside the prospect's turn. Role was read from content throughout. Transcription also garbles words — 'cowbell' for kettlebell, 'Monjaro'/'Ozempec' for Mounjaro/Ozempic, 'rota cuff' for rotator cuff — and several profanities and numbers are dropped.
